translationRepairs: Ministers argued that the boy emperor required a regent and urged her to follow the precedent of Han Empress Dowager He.
Ministers argued that the boy emperor required a regent and urged her to follow the precedent of Han Empress Hexi (He-xi).
和熹 is the posthumous title Hexi, not the surname He.
The assembled ministers memorialized: the Son of Heaven is young and tender; it is fitting to follow the precedent of Empress Dowager He of Han.
The assembled ministers memorialized: the Son of Heaven is young and tender; it is fitting to follow the precedent of Empress Hexi of Han.
Same Hexi/He error in the literal line.
She died in the third month of the seventh year of her reign, aged twenty-one.
She died in the third month of the seventh year of Xiankang, aged twenty-one.
七年 continues 咸康; she was empress only six years (s0053).
Xuan district's Lingyang county was changed to Guangyang county.
Xuancheng's Lingyang county was changed to Guangyang county.
宣城 is Xuancheng commandery, not Xuan district.
Empress Du the Chenggong had the taboo personal name Lingyang; she was a person of Jingzhao and was the great-granddaughter of the General Who Guards the South, Yu.
Empress Du the Chenggong had the taboo personal name Lingyang; she was a person of Jingzhao and was the great-granddaughter of the General Who Guards the South, Du Yu.
預 is Du Yu; Yu alone hides the surname.
Minister Jiang Yi argued: "Her rank and title fall short of empress dowager, so she should not receive full ritual deference."
Minister Jiang You argued: "Her rank and title fall short of empress dowager, so she should not receive full ritual deference."
江逌 is Jiang You (Yóu), not Yi; the idiomatic surname-name rendering mismatches the Chinese given name.
Empress Chu, posthumously titled Kangxian (Healthy and Presented).
The parenthetical 'Healthy and Presented' is a misleading morpheme-by-morpheme gloss of the posthumous title 康獻, not an idiomatic English rendering.
My late sister-consort was yielding and gentle, ever seeking to follow Earth's way; she deferred to the court's wishes because she put the state first.
The late empress was yielding and gentle, ever seeking to follow Earth's way; she deferred to the court's wishes because she put the state first.
先后 means the former empress (Mingmu in this biography), not a sister-consort; the idiomatic kinship is invented.
Empress Yu the Xiaoxiao of the Deposed Emperor had the taboo personal name Daolian and was a person from Yanling in Yingchuan.
Empress Yu the Xiao, consort of the Deposed Emperor, had the taboo personal name Daolian and was a person from Yanling in Yingchuan.
Literal English doubles 孝 as Xiaoxiao; the source has one posthumous Xiao plus surname Yu.
The Empress Dowager for the Emperor was a cousin's wife; court deliberation doubted her mourning garments.
To the emperor the empress dowager was a cousin's wife, so court deliberation was uncertain what mourning garments he should wear.
Literal phrasing makes 疑其服 a doubt about garments rather than uncertainty over the emperor's mourning grade.
Following his testament and the precedents of the classics and of Emperor Xiaohuai of Han, I elevate her to Empress Dowager Jianwen."
Following his testament and the precedents of the Spring and Autumn Annals, of the two Han dynasties, and of Emperor Xiaohuai, I elevate her to Empress Dowager Jianwen."
二漢孝懷皇帝 is not clearly 'Emperor Xiaohuai of Han'; 陽秋 is the Spring and Autumn Annals, and 孝懷皇帝 may be a separate Jin precedent.
In the third year of Ningkang Huan Chong, Central Army general, and others wrote: "Heaven and earth depend on each other to bring forth the cosmos;
In the third year of Ningkang, Huan Chong, Central Army general, and others wrote: "Heaven and earth depend on each other to bring forth the cosmos;
Missing comma after the era year fuses Ningkang with Huan Chong into one name.
The lady of Tushan wed Yu and the Xia flourished;
The lady of Tushan became a consort and the Xia clan thereby prospered;
Chinese 塗山作儷 does not name Yu; the English invents that husband.

When Emperor Xiaowu succeeded in Xian'an 2 she was posthumously honored as Empress Shun and jointly buried at Gaoping Mausoleum; her father Wang Xia was posthumously granted Specially Advanced and Grand Master of Splendid Happiness, with concurrent Cavalier Attendant-in-Ordinary.
光祿大夫 is not 'Household Minister'; 合葬 does not say 'buried with him' by name, and 追贈 marks posthumous gifts.
Empress Wang's personal name was Shen'ai; she came from Linyi in Langya commandery.
Empress Wang the Anxi's personal name was Shen'ai; she came from Linyi in Langya commandery.
Chinese 安僖王皇后 includes the posthumous title Anxi omitted in the idiomatic English.
Lady Feng was slender grace; beauty lush and softly yielding.
Lady Fen was slender grace; beauty lush and softly yielding.
芬 is Fen; Feng is a mistranscription.
the round unfolds following sundial; paired with Xi radiance thereby equal brightness.'
The round (moon) follows the sundial's course; paired with solar radiance it shares equal brightness.
Literal English is ungrammatical, obscures 圓舒 as the moon, and includes a stray quote.

Her father was Guang; as an entertainer he entered service and served as Prefect of Pingchang.
The calque 'by entertainer' is not English and obscures 以倡進.
